### 0.2 Your first tensors on a GPU

A neural network is just tensor arithmetic. Here is a 3×3 matrix multiply on the GPU —
the same operation that, repeated billions of times, trains GPT.

a = torch.randn(3, 3, device=device)   # random 3x3 matrix, lives on the GPU
b = torch.randn(3, 3, device=device)
c = a @ b                              # matrix multiplication

print(c)
print("\nresult lives on:", c.device)

## Lab 1-1 — BPE From Scratch

The lecture's toy corpus: `low ×5 · lower ×2 · newest ×6 · widest ×3`

The algorithm (slide *BPE — The Algorithm*):
1. start from characters
2. count all **adjacent pairs**
3. **merge** the most frequent pair, record the rule
4. repeat

The full BPE training loop — this is the whole algorithm!

cells.src:
# The full BPE training loop — this is the whole algorithm!

def train_bpe(corpus, num_merges):
    merges = []
    for step in range(num_merges):
        pairs = get_pair_counts(corpus)
        if not pairs:
            break
        best = max(pairs, key=pairs.get)          # most frequent pair
        corpus = merge_pair(corpus, best)
        merges.append(best)
        print(f"merge {step+1}: {best}  (count={pairs[best]})")
    return corpus, merges

final_corpus, merges = train_bpe(dict(corpus), num_merges=8)

print("\nfinal corpus:")
for word, freq in final_corpus.items():
    print(f"  {' '.join(word):<20} x{freq}")

pages.title: Tokenize an UNSEEN word by replaying the learned merges in order.

cells.src:
# Tokenize an UNSEEN word by replaying the learned merges in order.

def bpe_tokenize(word, merges):
    symbols = list(word) + ["</w>"]
    for a, b in merges:                    # replay merges in training order
        i = 0
        while i < len(symbols) - 1:
            if symbols[i] == a and symbols[i + 1] == b:
                symbols[i:i + 2] = [a + b]
            else:
                i += 1
    return symbols

print("lowest  →", bpe_tokenize("lowest", merges))   # never seen in training!
print("newer   →", bpe_tokenize("newer", merges))
print("widow   →", bpe_tokenize("widow", merges))

## Lab 1-2 — Real Tokenizers & Fertility

Now the industrial-strength versions. Watch what happens to Korean.

from transformers import AutoTokenizer, PreTrainedTokenizerFast

# English-centric BPE
gpt2_tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("gpt2")
# Korean-trained BPE
kogpt_tok = PreTrainedTokenizerFast.from_pretrained(
    "skt/kogpt2-base-v2",
    bos_token="</s>",
    eos_token="</s>",
    unk_token="<unk>",
    pad_token="<pad>",
    mask_token="<mask>",
)

en = "The weather is really nice today."
ko = "오늘은 날씨가 정말 좋네요."

for name, tok in [("GPT-2 (EN-centric)", gpt2_tok), ("KoGPT-2 (KO-trained)", kogpt_tok)]:
    print(f"=== {name} ===")
    for s in (en, ko):
        tokens = tok.tokenize(s)
        print(f"  {len(tokens):>2} tokens ← {s}")
        print(f"     {tokens}")
    print()

pages.title: Fertility = tokens per whitespace word. Compute it for both tokenizers on both s

cells.src:
# Fertility = tokens per whitespace word. Compute it for both tokenizers on both sentences.

def fertility(tokenizer, sentence):
    n_tokens = len(tokenizer.tokenize(sentence))
    n_words = len(sentence.split())
    return n_tokens / n_words

for name, tok in [("GPT-2", gpt2_tok), ("KoGPT-2", kogpt_tok)]:
    print(f"{name:<8} EN fertility = {fertility(tok, en):.2f}   KO fertility = {fertility(tok, ko):.2f}")

## Lab 1-3 — Train Your Own Korean Tokenizer

Let's fix it ourselves: train a BPE tokenizer **on Korean data**.
Data: **NSMC** (Naver Sentiment Movie Corpus) — 150k Korean movie reviews, the classic Korean NLP dataset.

import pandas as pd

# NSMC: id / document / label (0=negative, 1=positive)
url = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/e9t/nsmc/master/ratings_train.txt"
nsmc = pd.read_csv(url, sep="\t").dropna()

print(nsmc.shape)
nsmc.head()

pages.title: from tokenizers import Tokenizer, models, trainers, pre_tokenizers

cells.src:
from tokenizers import Tokenizer, models, trainers, pre_tokenizers

texts = nsmc["document"].astype(str).tolist()

# Build a BPE tokenizer and train it on the 150k Korean reviews
my_tok = Tokenizer(models.BPE(unk_token="[UNK]"))
my_tok.pre_tokenizer = pre_tokenizers.Whitespace()

trainer = trainers.BpeTrainer(
    vocab_size=8000,
    special_tokens=["[UNK]", "[PAD]"],
)
my_tok.train_from_iterator(texts, trainer)

print("vocab size:", my_tok.get_vocab_size())

print(f"our Korean BPE : {len(enc.tokens):>2} tokens → {enc.tokens}")
print(f"GPT-2          : {len(gpt2_tok.tokenize(ko)):>2} tokens")

# and on review-style text it has actually seen the style of:
sample = "이 영화 진짜 재미있어요 배우들 연기가 대박"
print(f"\nour Korean BPE : {my_tok.encode(sample).tokens}")

## Lab 1-4 — word2vec on Real Korean Data

Now the second half of the lecture: **from tokens to vectors.**
We train skip-gram word2vec on the NSMC reviews and explore the space it learns.

from gensim.models import Word2Vec
import re

# Sentences for word2vec: for simplicity, split each review on whitespace with eliminating punctuation
sentences = []

for t in texts:
    # punctuation
    t = re.sub(r"[^가-힣A-Za-z0-9\s]", " ", t)
    # whitespace split
    tokens = t.split()
    sentences.append(tokens)

w2v = Word2Vec(
    sentences,
    vector_size=100,   # d — embedding dimension
    window=5,          # m — context window size
    min_count=5,       # ignore very rare words
    sg=1,              # 1 = skip-gram (the lecture's variant), 0 = CBOW
    negative=10,       # k negative samples
    workers=4,
    seed=42,
)

print("vocabulary size:", len(w2v.wv))
print("vector for '영화':", w2v.wv["영화"][:8], "…")

pages.title: Nearest neighbors — "you shall know a word by the company it keeps"

# Nearest neighbors — "you shall know a word by the company it keeps"
for query in ["영화", "배우", "최고", "쓰레기"]:
    neighbors = w2v.wv.most_similar(query, topn=5)
    pretty = ", ".join(f"{w}({s:.2f})" for w, s in neighbors)
    print(f"{query:>4} → {pretty}")

Do similar words really cluster? Let's project 60 frequent words to 2-D with PCA.

pages.title: import numpy as np

cells.src:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA

words = [w for w, _ in sorted(w2v.wv.key_to_index.items(), key=lambda kv: kv[1])[:200]
         if len(w) >= 2][:60]
vecs = np.array([w2v.wv[w] for w in words])

xy = PCA(n_components=2).fit_transform(vecs)

plt.figure(figsize=(11, 7))
plt.scatter(xy[:, 0], xy[:, 1], s=12, color="#2C5F9E")
for (x, y), w in zip(xy, words):
    plt.annotate(w, (x, y), fontsize=10, alpha=0.85)
plt.title("word2vec on NSMC — 60 frequent words, PCA to 2-D")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
